sources.note: Wordlist only in practical orthography (ni'aba 'eye', wa'ai 'dog', mo'o 'banana'); no stress marks.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Bauwaki language' (downloaded 2026-09-17); Ethnologue free page for bwk (downloaded via r.jina.ai)

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide, 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Sec. 2.3.1.25 Mailuan.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content for Bauwaki; states documentation level = wordlist only (Anonymous 1913, Ray 1938); gives Proto-Mailuan pronouns (Ross) and a few Bauwaki reflexes of pTNG etyma (baba 'father', idi 'hair', ibi 'name', iini- 'sleep').

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2017. Farming and the Trans-New Guinea family: a consideration. In Martine Robbeets & Alexander Savelyev (eds), Language Dispersal Beyond Farming, 155-181. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/z.215 (volume; OAPEN 20.500.12657/29648).
sources.note: one banana etymon cited; no phonology of Bauwaki

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur (collector). n.d. [catalogued 1999]. Vocabulary of language spoken at Keveri (Bauwaki). 9-page typed Motu elicitation schedule 'Gado ladana: Keveri' with pencilled Bauwaki responses, a pronoun/verb paradigm page and 71 Motu test sentences (c. 15 answered). PARADISEC item AC2-PNGNPBAU101, doi:10.4225/72/56EACDD054AD4 (Capell fieldnotes image site, CC BY-NC-SA).
sources.note: No prose. Pencilled transcriptions mark glottal stop with an apostrophe/raised stroke (ni'aba, va'ai, deba'a, word-initial 'orani, 'amari, 'ila) and vowel quality with IPA-like symbols (kɔkɔrɔ, ɛmɛ); no accent marks, length marks or any note on stress or tone. An isolated raised stroke before consonant-initial 'kɔkɔrɔ on p.1/1 cannot be read as a stress mark.

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: ANU. Language index s.v. 'Bauwaki (SE Oro & Central Provs; also Bawaki; see Oiwa)'.
sources.note: No phonology content; establishes that no grammar, phonology, or stress-marked wordlist manuscript for Bauwaki was known to the most complete New Guinea bibliography as of 1995.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom. 1996. Lau'una: another Austronesian remnant on the south-east coast of Papua. In John Lynch & Fa'afo Pat (eds), Oceanic studies: proceedings of the First International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, 61-82. Pacific Linguistics C-133. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: map label only; nothing on phonology

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom. 1982. Borrowing in Austronesian and non-Austronesian languages of coastal south-east mainland Papua New Guinea. In A. Halim, L. Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 109-177. Pacific Linguistics C-74. doi:10.15144/PL-C74.109
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Appendix 2 'Mailuan phonemes and the reconstruction of Proto-Mailuan' pp.162-163 is the only phonological treatment of Bauwaki: tentative synchronic segment chart from survey wordlists (Bauwaki: p/f, t/s, k [not medially], b, d, g, h, m, n, l/r, v/w, y; five vowels i e a o u); 'All languages have open syllables and there are no consonant clusters'; fn.34 p.172: Bauwaki drops final vowels after m, n. a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/prosod: 0 relevant hits.

sources.citation: Dutton, T. E. 1976. Austronesian languages: eastern part of south-eastern mainland Papua. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages, 321-333. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: Australian National University. (hdl 1885/253001)
sources.note: No phonology content on Bauwaki: the language appears only in a population table (p.324). The chapter's phonological remarks concern Austronesian Magori-group interference from Mailuan/Dagan neighbours in general terms; a full-text search for stress/accent/tone/tonal returns nothing.

sources.citation: Dutton, T. E. 1975. South-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 613-664. Pacific Linguistics C-38. doi:10.15144/PL-C38.613
sources.note: Only a phylum-wide sentence, sec. 2.9.3.1 'Phonological aspects' p.622, covering all South-East Trans-New Guinea languages with 'no attempt.. to distinguish characteristics of individual families': 'Some languages are tonal but stress is generally important and related to intonation which may be quite complex.' Not about Bauwaki. Sec. 2.9.5.5 p.638: 'None of the languages except Magi (or Mailu) has been studied or recorded in any detail.' Bauwaki entry 2.9.5.5.5 p.639 gives territory, 'a kind of bridge language between the Mailuan and Yareban Families', name pronounced bavake 'true speech'; n…

sources.citation: Thomson, N. P. 1975. Magi phonology and grammar -- fifty years afterwards. In T. E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in languages of central and south-east Papua, 599-666. Pacific Linguistics C-29. doi:10.15144/PL-C29.599
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Sister language Magi/Mailu only (sec. 2.5 Stress pp.605-606: usually penultimate, sometimes antepenultimate, never final in polysyllables). Bauwaki not mentioned anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing). Recorded as the nearest described relative, not as a Bauwaki source.

sources.citation: Williams, F. E. 1944. Mission influence amongst the Keveri of south-east Papua. Oceania 15(2): 89-141. doi:10.1002/j.1834-4461.1944.tb00415.x (open scanned text: archive.org sim_oceania_1944-12_15_2).
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnography of Kwato mission influence among the Keveri; linguistic content limited to group/dialect names and the remark that prayers are said 'in the real Keveri language, though pidgin Motuan is so well known'. Searched for accent, stress, syllable, vocabulary, dialect, tone: no phonological content.
